title: An (almost) efficient classical algorithm for sampling from typical Gibbs states
abstract: Gibbs state preparation has emerged as a potential avenue for quantum advantage in the study of physical systems. Although there is known advantage for computing local properties of worst-case Gibbs states, recent results suggest a different picture for average-case local systems: at temperatures where their Gibbs states can be efficiently prepared quantumly, quasi-polynomial time classical algorithms can also compute local expectation values. Yet this leaves open the possibility of an advantage under a stronger notion of simulation: sampling. Gibbs sampling underlies Boltzmann machine-based quantum learning algorithms and quantum supremacy proposals, but its classical average-case complexity for physically relevant models remains unresolved. Here, we give strong evidence against an exponential quantum advantage in Gibbs sampling for an ensemble of local systems known as the quantum $p$-spin model. We describe a classical algorithm for sampling from the Gibbs state to any polynomially small error in total variation distance. Our algorithm is based on a meta-algorithm known as algorithmic stochastic localization (ASL). Our main technical result is a generalized convergence theorem for ASL which reduces approximate sampling from any distribution on the hypercube to estimating the mean of a related "tilted distribution" to sufficiently low additive error. We then extend known quasi-polynomial time algorithms for computing local expectation values of a related disordered model to compute these "tilted means" for the quantum $p$-spin model. Finally, we give a non-rigorous physics argument that this mean-estimation algorithm works down to the spin glass transition temperature. As efficient quantum algorithms also fail at this transition, this suggests they cannot Gibbs sample the quantum $p$-spin model at temperatures below that for which classical algorithms are also (almost) efficient.
summary: This paper develops a classical algorithm to sample from the Gibbs state of the quantum p-spin model, showing that the process can be reduced to estimating 'tilted means' using advanced mathematical techniques. The authors argue that this classical efficiency suggests that quantum computers may not offer an exponential advantage for sampling these typical disordered systems, particularly near phase transitions.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether there is an exponential quantum advantage over classical algorithms for sampling from the Gibbs state of typical local Hamiltonians.
main_result: The authors provide strong evidence against an exponential quantum advantage in Gibbs sampling for the quantum p-spin model, suggesting classical algorithms can achieve sampling efficiency down to the spin glass transition temperature.
method: The classical algorithm is constructed using Algorithmic Stochastic Localization (ASL), which reduces sampling to estimating the mean of a related 'tilted distribution' using techniques derived from Barvinok's interpolation method.
model_or_system: The primary model is the quantum p-spin model, an ensemble of local Hamiltonians defined by random Gaussian couplings. The analysis focuses on the thermal Gibbs state associated with this Hamiltonian.
key_observables: Total Variation Distance (TVD) between the true Gibbs distribution and the sampled distribution; the 'tilted mean' of the distribution.
important_parameters: Temperature (especially near the spin glass transition), system size N, and the error tolerance $\epsilon$.
main_assumptions: The final argument regarding the spin glass transition temperature is noted as a non-rigorous physics argument; the rigorous convergence proof relies on the zero-freeness of the tilted partition function in the complex plane.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of quantum advantage in Gibbs sampling, develops the ASL meta-algorithm, proves a general convergence theorem for ASL based on estimating tilted means, and applies this to the quantum p-spin model to draw conclusions about computational complexity.
why_interesting: It directly addresses the boundary between quantum simulation and classical computation for equilibrium statistical mechanics, which is a major theme in modern condensed matter theory.
